question: In the 2015 life table constructed from 299,555 dogs insured in Japan between April 2010 and March 2011, what was the overall life expectancy of dogs?
answer: 13.7 years.

evidence.title: A current life table and causes of death for insured dogs in Japan.
evidence.quote: The life expectancies and causes of death were evaluated in 299,555 dogs insured in Japan between 1 April 2010 and 31 March 2011, of which 4169 dogs died during this period. The overall life expectancy of dogs was 13.7 years.

question: In the 2018 owner-survey study of mortality in 5,663 deceased UK Kennel Club-registered dogs, which breeds had the longest and the shortest median longevity, and what were the values?
answer: Longest: West Highland Terrier (12.71 years); shortest: Dobermann Pinscher (7.67 years). Overall median age at death was 10.33 years.

evidence.title: Longevity and mortality in Kennel Club registered dog breeds in the UK in 2014.
evidence.quote: Overall median age at death was 10.33 years (interquartile range: 7.17-12.83 years). Breeds varied widely in median longevity overall from the West Highland Terrier (12.71 years) to the Dobermann Pinscher (7.67 years).

question: In the 2022 VetCompass life-table study of UK companion dogs, based on 30,563 dogs that died between January 2016 and July 2020, what was the estimated life expectancy at age 0 for all dogs?

evidence.title: Life tables of annual life expectancy and mortality for companion dogs in the United Kingdom.
evidence.quote: Among 30,563 dogs that died between 1st January 2016 and 31st July 2020, life expectancy at age 0 was 11.23 [95% confidence interval (CI): 11.19-11.27] years.

question: In the 2023 study that generated life expectancy tables for dogs and cats from Banfield Pet Hospital clinical records in the USA (survey years 2013-2019), what was the life expectancy at birth for all dogs?

evidence.title: Life expectancy tables for dogs and cats derived from clinical data.
evidence.quote: LE at birth (LEbirth) was 12.69 years (95% CI: 12.68-12.70) for all dogs, 12.71 years (12.67-12.76) for mixed-breed dogs, 11.18 years (11.16-11.20) for cats, and 11.12 (11.09-11.14) for mixed-breed cats.

question: In the analysis of 137,469 dogs that died in Switzerland between 2016 and 2020 (Amicus national database), what was the mean life expectancy of brachycephalic dogs, and how much shorter was it than that of mesocephalic and dolichocephalic dogs?
answer: 9.8 years; 2.1 years less than mesocephalic dogs and 1.7 years less than dolichocephalic dogs.

evidence.title: [Life expectancy of mesocephalic, dolichocephalic and brachycephalic dog breeds in Switzerland].
evidence.quote: The mean life expectancy of brachycephalic dogs was 9,8 years, i.e., 2,1 and 1,7 years less than mesocephalic and dolichocephalic dogs, respectively.

notes: Decimal commas in the source (9,8; 2,1; 1,7) correspond to 9.8, 2.1 and 1.7 years.

question: According to the 2024 review that examined dog aging and mortality studies spanning about 40 years (1981 to 2023) to assess how average dog lifespan is reported, has the median lifespan of domesticated dogs recently decreased, as claimed in the popular press?
answer: No. The review concluded that median lifespan has not recently decreased but rather has increased steadily over that time frame.

evidence.title: How can we achieve more accurate reporting of average dog lifespan?
evidence.quote: However, in examining several different kinds of dog aging and mortality studies covering a span of about 40 years (1981 to 2023), it seems apparent that the median lifespan of domesticated dogs has not recently decreased, as has been reported in the popular press, but rather has increased steadily over that time frame.

question: In the 2013 analysis of 5,095 confirmed deaths among 102,609 owned dogs attending first-opinion veterinary practices in central and southeast England, by how many years did the longevity of crossbred dogs exceed that of purebred dogs in multivariable modelling, and what was the direction of the association between bodyweight and longevity?
answer: Crossbred dogs outlived purebreds by 1.2 years (95% CI 0.9-1.4; P<0.001); increasing bodyweight was negatively correlated with longevity.

evidence.title: Longevity and mortality of owned dogs in England.
evidence.quote: The results of multivariable modelling indicated that longevity in crossbred dogs exceeded purebred dogs by 1.2 years (95% confidence interval 0.9-1.4; P<0.001) and that increasing bodyweight was negatively correlated with longevity.

question: In the 2013 analysis that fitted mortality hazard models to death data from 74 dog breeds to decompose the size-lifespan trade-off, which mortality component was identified as the driving force behind the shorter lifespan of large dogs, and was body size clearly correlated with the onset of senescence?
answer: A strong positive relationship between body size and aging rate (large dogs die young mainly because they age quickly); no clear correlation between body size and onset of senescence was found, and baseline hazard was only slightly higher in large dogs.

evidence.title: The size-life span trade-off decomposed: why large dogs die young.
evidence.quote: We did not find a clear correlation between body size and the onset of senescence. The baseline hazard is slightly higher in large dogs, but the driving force behind the trade-off between size and life span is apparently a strong positive relationship between size and aging rate.

question: In the 2015 life table of dogs insured in Japan, life expectancy was reported for five body-weight groups (<5 kg, 5-10 kg, 10-20 kg, 20-40 kg and >=40 kg). Which group had the highest life expectancy, and what was its value?
answer: The 5-10 kg group, at 14.2 years; the <5 kg group (13.8 years) was the exception to the decline of life expectancy with increasing body weight.

evidence.title: A current life table and causes of death for insured dogs in Japan.
evidence.quote: The life expectancy was 13.8 years in the <5 kg body weight group, 14.2 years in the 5-10 kg body weight group, 13.6 years in the 10-20 kg body weight group, 12.5 years in the 20-40 kg body weight group and 10.6 years in the ≥40 kg body weight group. As body weight increases, life expectancy tended to decrease except in the <5 kg body weight group.

question: In the 2020 study of 20,970 privately owned dogs seen at three independent primary care veterinary clinics in the United States, by how much shorter were the median survival times of breeds in the "Mountain" ancestral group compared with other purebred dog groups, and did the difference persist after correcting for body size?
answer: 3.5-4.6 years shorter; yes, the difference remained significant even when correcting for body size.

evidence.title: Lifespan of companion dogs seen in three independent primary care veterinary clinics in the United States.
evidence.quote: We also found that dog breeds belonging to the "Mountain" ancestral group had median survival times that were 3.5-4.6 years shorter than other purebred dog groups, which remained significant even when correcting for body size.

question: In the 2023 Banfield study that generated life expectancy tables for dogs and cats from clinical records of more than 1,000 US hospitals, which life-table method was used, and how were survivors defined for each survey year?
answer: Sullivan's method; survivors were animals with no death date recorded in that survey year who were confirmed living by a veterinary visit in a subsequent year.

evidence.title: Life expectancy tables for dogs and cats derived from clinical data.
evidence.quote: Using Sullivan's method, LE tables were generated across survey years 2013-2019, by survey year, and for subpopulations defined by sex, adult body size group (purebred dogs only: toy, small, medium, large and giant), and median body condition score (BCS) over life. The deceased population for each survey year comprised animals with a recorded date of death in that year; survivors had no death date in that year and were confirmed living by a veterinary visit in a subsequent year.

question: Both the 2022 VetCompass life-table study of UK companion dogs and the 2024 study of life expectancy at birth using Portugal's national registry (278,116 dogs) identified the breed with the lowest life expectancy at birth. Which breed was it in each study, and what were the two estimates as reported in each study's abstract?
answer: French Bulldog in both studies: 4.53 years (95% CI 4.14-5.01) in the UK and 6.27 years in Portugal.

evidence.title: Life tables of annual life expectancy and mortality for companion dogs in the United Kingdom.
evidence.quote: Jack Russell Terrier (12.72 years; 95% CI: 12.53-12.90) and French Bulldog (4.53 years; 95% CI: 4.14-5.01) had the longest and shortest life expectancy at age 0, respectively.

evidence.title: Investigating the Life Expectancy at Birth of Companion Dogs in Portugal Using Official National Registry Data.
evidence.quote: The analysis of life expectancy at birth for the 20 most common non-Portuguese breeds and 10 Portuguese breeds revealed that Yorkshire Terriers had the highest life expectancy (10.89 years) and French Bulldogs the lowest (6.27 years).

notes: The Portuguese full text (Table 2 section) reports 6.29 years for the French Bulldog and 11.7 years for the Yorkshire Terrier, which differs slightly from the abstract values; the gold answer follows the abstract.

review.issue: The Portuguese paper's full text reports 6.29 years for the French Bulldog (Results text and Table 2) while its abstract, which the evidence quote and gold answer follow, says 6.27; the question should pin the answer to the abstracts so a full-text-informed answer of 6.29 is not wrongly graded against it.

question: In the 2024 UK study of 584,734 dogs (284,734 deceased) that estimated Kaplan-Meier median survival separately for purebred and crossbred dogs, what were the two median survival estimates, and which group lived longer?
answer: Purebreds 12.7 years versus crossbreds 12.0 years; purebreds lived longer (crossbred hazard ratio 1.1, p<0.001).

evidence.title: Longevity of companion dog breeds: those at risk from early death.
evidence.quote: Median survival for pure breeds was 12.7 years (12.6-12.7, n = 473,681, events = 212,289), whilst median survival for crossbreds was 12.0 years (12.0-12.1, n = 111,053, events = 72,445, HR 1.1, 1.1-1.1, p < 0.001).

notes: Notable because it runs counter to the usual crossbred longevity advantage reported in other datasets (e.g. the 2013 England VetCompass analysis).

question: In the 2025 life-table study of companion dogs from six veterinary hospitals in Seoul, South Korea, life expectancy at age 1 was higher than at age 0. What were the two life expectancy values, and what pattern of mortality explains the difference?
answer: 9.390 years at age 0 versus 10.123 years at age 1; the probability of dying between ages 0 and 1 was 0.161, whereas from age 1 to age 10 the probability of dying at each age was below 0.1.

evidence.title: Life expectancy and survival analysis for companion dogs and cats in Seoul, South Korea.
evidence.quote: In the life tables created for the dog and cat study populations, the life expectancy at age 0 was 9.390 years in dogs and 5.384 in cats. The probability of a dog dying between the ages of 0 and 1 year was 0.161. After age 1 until age 10, the probability of dying at each age was <0.1, so the dog's life expectancy was higher at age 1 (10.123 years) than at age 0 (9.390 years).

question: In the 2008 SNP-based association mapping of breed stereotypes using DNA from 148 dog breeds, how many significant loci were identified for longevity, and how was longevity described in relation to breed selection and breed size?
answer: 4 significant loci; longevity was described as a breed characteristic not under direct selection but inversely correlated with breed size.

evidence.title: Single-nucleotide-polymorphism-based association mapping of dog stereotypes.
evidence.quote: Four significant loci were identified for longevity, a breed characteristic not under direct selection, but inversely correlated with breed size.

evidence.title: Single-nucleotide-polymorphism-based association mapping of dog stereotypes.
evidence.quote: We used DNA samples isolated from 148 dog breeds to associate SNP markers with breed stereotypes.

question: In the 2020 study of body size, inbreeding, and lifespan in domestic dogs, which estimated life expectancies for pure and mixed breed dogs from the Veterinary Medical Database and other published sources, how much longer on average did mixed breed dogs live than size-matched purebred dogs?
answer: About 1.2 years longer.

evidence.title: Body size, inbreeding, and lifespan in domestic dogs.
evidence.quote: When comparing mixed versus purebred dogs, however, mixed breed dogs lived about 1.2 years longer on average than size-matched purebred dogs.

question: In the genome-wide association study of long-lived Cane Corso dogs, SNPs in which four genes were concluded to be associated with longevity?
answer: TDRP, MC2R, FBXO25 and FBXL21.

evidence.title: Four novel genes associated with longevity found in Cane corso purebred dogs.
evidence.quote: We conclude that genes TDRP, MC2R, FBXO25 and FBXL21 are associated with longevity in Cane corso dogs.

question: In the 2007 analysis of 77 American Kennel Club breeds (data on more than 700 dogs) relating breed height and weight to life span, what were the correlation coefficients of height and of weight with longevity, and which variable was the significant predictor of life span in the regression?
answer: Height r = -0.603 and weight r = -0.679 (both negative, p<0.05); weight was the significant predictor of life span (p<0.001).

evidence.title: Statistical analysis regarding the effects of height and weight on life span of the domestic dog.
evidence.quote: A negative correlation was observed between height and longevity (r=-0.603, p<0.05), and between weight and longevity (r=-0.679, p<0.05). Weight was the significant predictor of life span (p<0.001), revealing that breeds smaller by weight generally live longer than heavier breeds.

evidence.title: Statistical analysis regarding the effects of height and weight on life span of the domestic dog.
evidence.quote: Seventy-seven American Kennel Club breeds were analyzed with data collected for more than 700 dogs.

question: In the 2009 genetic mapping of fixed breed phenotypes across 147 dog breeds, which three disease conditions were associated with a specific IGF1 haplotype, demonstrating the approach's power to map loci regulating polygenic disease incidence?
answer: Hip dysplasia, patella luxation, and pancreatitis.

evidence.title: Genetic mapping of fixed phenotypes: disease frequency as a breed characteristic.
evidence.quote: The power of this approach to identify loci regulating the incidence of specific polygenic diseases is demonstrated by the association of a specific IGF1 haplotype with hip dysplasia, patella luxation, and pancreatitis.

evidence.title: Genetic mapping of fixed phenotypes: disease frequency as a breed characteristic.
evidence.quote: DNA samples from 147 dog breeds were used to characterize single nucleotide polymorphism allele frequencies for association mapping of breed stereotypes.

question: In the 2020 scan for genes associated with cancer mortality and longevity in pedigree dog breeds (phenotypic data from more than 72,000 dogs combined with a large genotypic dataset), within which gene was the single variant marginally associated with body-weight-corrected longevity residuals located, and what kind of protein does that gene encode?
answer: PRDX1, which encodes a peroxiredoxin (described as belonging to an emerging class of pro-longevity associated genes).

evidence.title: A scan for genes associated with cancer mortality and longevity in pedigree dog breeds.
evidence.quote: One putative genetic variant was marginally significantly associated with longevity residuals that had been corrected for the effects of body weight; this genetic variant is located within PRDX1, a peroxiredoxin that belongs to an emerging class of pro-longevity associated genes.

evidence.title: A scan for genes associated with cancer mortality and longevity in pedigree dog breeds.
evidence.quote: We combine phenotypic data from > 72,000 dogs with a large genotypic dataset to search for genes associated with cancer mortality and longevity in pedigree dog breeds.

question: In the 2023 analysis of how body size and genetic diversity (heterozygosity) shape lifespan across 118 purebred dog breeds (more than 40,000 dogs with owner-reported lifespan and cause of death), what bias did the authors identify in available breed-specific lifespan estimates, and how did they remove it?
answer: A right-censoring bias: early-dying dogs from birth cohorts that had not completely died off are sampled disproportionately, especially in rapidly growing breeds. They removed it by including only completed birth cohorts.

evidence.title: How size and genetic diversity shape lifespan across breeds of purebred dogs.
evidence.quote: We hypothesized that this might be due to a strong right-censoring bias in available breed-specific lifespan estimates where early-dying dogs from birth cohorts that have not died off completely at the time of data collection are sampled disproportionately, especially in breeds with rapidly growing populations.

evidence.title: How size and genetic diversity shape lifespan across breeds of purebred dogs.
evidence.quote: After documenting and removing the right-censoring bias from the breed-specific lifespan estimates by including only completed birth cohorts in our analyses, we show that small size and genetic diversity are both linked to a significant increase in mean lifespan across breeds.

question: In the Golden Retriever GWAS that implicated a 5'UTR variant of ERBB4 in lifespan, when all 304 dogs were analyzed together, what were the survival times of dogs homozygous for haplotype 3 versus dogs homozygous for haplotype 1?
answer: 11.6 years for haplotype 3 homozygotes (shortest) versus 13.5 years for haplotype 1 homozygotes (longest), p = 0.0008.

evidence.title: A variant in the 5'UTR of ERBB4 is associated with lifespan in Golden Retrievers.
evidence.quote: When all GR dogs were analyzed together (n = 304), the presence of haplotype 3 was associated with shorter survival (11.8 years vs. 12.8 years, p = 0.024). GRs homozygous for haplotype 3 had the shortest survival, and GRs homozygous for haplotype 1 had the longest survival (11.6 years vs. 13.5 years, p = 0.0008).

question: In the study connecting serum IGF-1, body size, and age in the domestic dog (animals from a few months to 204 months of age and 5 to 160 lb, analyzed in four sex/neuter groups), how did serum IGF-1 relate to age and to body weight?
answer: IGF-1 decreased with age in all groups, with significant male-female differences; overall, IGF-1 increased with increasing weight, although the IGF-1-weight relationship differed by spay/neuter status.

evidence.title: Connecting serum IGF-1, body size, and age in the domestic dog.
evidence.quote: IGF-1 loss over time, as a function of age, decreases in all groups with significant differences between males and females. The relationship between IGF-1 and weight differs depending upon spay/neuter status, but there is an overall increase in IGF-1 levels with increasing weight.

question: In the 2020 scan for genes associated with cancer mortality and longevity in pedigree dog breeds, after cancer mortality was corrected for body weight, what was the direction of the correlation between breed life span and the cancer mortality residuals, and what did the authors say this implies?
answer: A significant positive correlation: after correcting for body weight, long-lived breeds die more frequently from cancer than short-lived breeds.

evidence.title: A scan for genes associated with cancer mortality and longevity in pedigree dog breeds.
evidence.quote: We identified a significant positive correlation between life span and cancer mortality residuals corrected for body weight, implying that long-lived breeds die more frequently from cancer compared to short-lived breeds.

notes: Counter-intuitive finding: once body weight is removed, longer-lived breeds show higher cancer mortality, presumably because they survive to ages at which cancer dominates.

question: In the 2020 study of body size, inbreeding, and lifespan in domestic dogs (genome-wide SNP-based inbreeding for over 100 breeds plus pedigree data for over 9000 golden retrievers), how did the across-breed relationship between inbreeding and life expectancy differ from the within-breed relationship, and how did the authors interpret the contrast?
answer: Across breeds, inbreeding was not associated with life expectancy once size was controlled; within golden retrievers, individual pedigree inbreeding negatively impacted lifespan. Interpretation: recent (within-breed) inbreeding is more likely to affect fitness than historic (among-breed) inbreeding.

evidence.title: Body size, inbreeding, and lifespan in domestic dogs.
evidence.quote: When controlling for size, variation in inbreeding was not associated with life expectancy across breeds. When comparing mixed versus purebred dogs, however, mixed breed dogs lived about 1.2 years longer on average than size-matched purebred dogs. Furthermore, individual pedigree coefficients of inbreeding and lifespans for over 9000 golden retrievers showed that inbreeding does negatively impact lifespan at the individual level.

evidence.title: Body size, inbreeding, and lifespan in domestic dogs.
evidence.quote: Our results suggest that recent inbreeding, as reflected in variation within a breed, is more likely to affect fitness than historic inbreeding, as reflected in variation among breeds.

question: In the genome-wide association study of longevity in Cavalier King Charles Spaniels (long-lived dogs defined as older than 13 years), how many dogs in each group and how many variants were used in the association analysis after initial data clean-up?
answer: 41 dogs (24 long-lived and 17 reference) and 92,679 variants.

evidence.title: Identification of genes associated with longevity in dogs: 9 candidate genes described in Cavalier King Charles Spaniel.
evidence.quote: After initial data clean-up, 92,679 variants and 41 dogs (24 long-lived and 17 reference) were used for the association analysis.

evidence.title: Identification of genes associated with longevity in dogs: 9 candidate genes described in Cavalier King Charles Spaniel.
evidence.quote: This genome-wide association study (GWAS) was undertaken to identify the candidate genes associated with longevity in Cavalier King Charles Spaniel individuals that have reached the age of more than 13 years.

question: How is the design of the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD) clinical trial characterised, and from what population are its healthy middle-aged dogs recruited?
answer: A parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial; dogs are recruited from Dog Aging Project participants.

evidence.title: Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD): study design and rationale for a prospective, parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial of rapamycin in healthy middle-aged dogs from the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: The Test of Rapamycin In Aging Dogs (TRIAD) randomized clinical trial is a parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial that will test the ability of rapamycin to prolong lifespan and improve several healthspan metrics in healthy, middle-aged dogs recruited from Dog Aging Project participants.

question: In the 2017 randomized controlled trial of short-term rapamycin in 24 middle-aged companion dogs, which three echocardiographic measures suggested improvement in age-related heart function in the rapamycin-treated dogs?
answer: E/A ratio, fractional shortening, and ejection fraction (covering both diastolic and systolic measures).

evidence.title: A randomized controlled trial to establish effects of short-term rapamycin treatment in 24 middle-aged companion dogs.
evidence.quote: Echocardiography suggested improvement in both diastolic and systolic age-related measures of heart function (E/A ratio, fractional shortening, and ejection fraction) in the rapamycin-treated dogs.

question: In the 2023 masked, placebo-controlled, randomized trial of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy client-owned dogs, what rapamycin dose was used, how often was it given, and for how long?
answer: 0.025 mg/kg, administered three times per week for 6 months.

evidence.title: A masked, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial evaluating safety and the effect on cardiac function of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy client-owned dogs.
evidence.quote: Low-dose rapamycin (0.025 mg/kg) or placebo was administered three times per week for 6 months.

question: In the lifetime diet restriction study of 48 Labrador retrievers, in which one dog of each pair was fed 25% less than its pair-mate from 8 weeks of age, by how much was median lifespan extended in the diet-restricted dogs?
answer: Median lifespan was 1.8 years longer in the diet-restricted dogs, with delayed onset of late-life diseases, especially osteoarthritis.

evidence.title: Diet restriction and ageing in the dog: major observations over two decades.
evidence.quote: Labrador retrievers (n 48) were paired at age 6 weeks by sex and weight within each of seven litters, and assigned randomly within the pair to control-feeding (CF) or 25 % diet restriction (DR). Feeding began at age 8 weeks. The same diet was fed to all dogs; only the quantity differed. Major lifetime observations included 1.8 years longer median lifespan among diet-restricted dogs, with delayed onset of late life diseases, especially osteoarthritis.

question: In the placebo-controlled L-deprenyl (selegiline) survival study in beagles, how many dogs were enrolled, into how many pairs were they allotted, and what oral dose and treatment duration were used?
answer: 82 beagles allotted to 41 pairs; 1 mg/kg L-deprenyl (or placebo) orally once daily for 2 years and 10 weeks.

evidence.title: Treatment with L-deprenyl prolongs life in elderly dogs.
evidence.quote: Eighty two beagle dogs ranging in age from 2.8 to 16.4 years and in weight from 6.3 to 15.8 kg were allotted to 41 pairs and administered placebo or 1 mg/kg L-deprenyl orally once daily for 2 years and 10 weeks.

question: In the 2002 paired-feeding study of 25% diet restriction in 48 Labrador Retrievers, how were median life span and maximum life span defined?
answer: Median life span was the age when 50% of the dogs were deceased; maximum life span was the age when 90% of the dogs were deceased.

evidence.title: Effects of diet restriction on life span and age-related changes in dogs.
evidence.quote: Age at onset of chronic disease and median (age when 50% of the dogs were deceased) and maximum (age when 90% of the dogs were deceased) life spans were evaluated.

question: In the 2023 placebo-controlled trial of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy client-owned dogs, in what percentage of the bi-weekly owner surveys were perceived positive changes in behavior or health reported for rapamycin-treated dogs, compared with placebo-treated dogs?
answer: 26.8% of surveys for rapamycin-treated dogs versus 8.1% for placebo-treated dogs.

evidence.title: A masked, placebo-controlled, randomized clinical trial evaluating safety and the effect on cardiac function of low-dose rapamycin in 17 healthy client-owned dogs.
evidence.quote: In 26.8% of the bi-weekly surveys owners whose dogs received rapamycin reported perceived positive changes in behavior or health, compared to 8.1% in the placebo group

notes: The abstract reports p = 0.04 for this comparison; the p-value is outside the cited span.

question: In the 90-day prospective, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of diets containing medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) plus a Brain Protection Blend (BPB) in 87 client-owned dogs with signs of cognitive dysfunction syndrome, which diet significantly improved all 6 categories of CDS signs, and in how many categories did the control diet improve?
answer: The 6.5% MCT oil + BPB diet improved all 6 categories; the control diet improved in only 4 of 6 categories.

evidence.title: Efficacy of a Therapeutic Diet on Dogs With Signs of Cognitive Dysfunction Syndrome (CDS): A Prospective Double Blinded Placebo Controlled Clinical Study.
evidence.quote: Eighty-seven dogs were randomly enrolled into one of three diet groups with 29 dogs per group: Control, 6.5% MCT oil + BPB (6.5% MCT diet), 9% MCT oil + BPB (9% MCT diet). Diets were fed for a period of 90 days, and each dog's CDS signs were re-evaluated at day 30 and day 90. All 6 categories of the CDS signs were significantly improved (p <0.05) in the dogs given the 6.5% MCT diet at the end of the 90-day study. Control only improved in 4 out 6 categories.

notes: The abstract's inline HTML italics tags are preserved verbatim in the quote because the validator matches the raw abstract text.

question: In the case report of an eight-year-old castrated male Labrador retriever that developed severe asymptomatic hypertriglyceridemia during six months of low-dose rapamycin, how long after rapamycin was discontinued did the lipemia and hypertriglyceridemia resolve, and what lipid-targeted treatment was required?
answer: They completely resolved within 15 days of stopping rapamycin, with no targeted lipemic intervention.

evidence.title: Case report: Severe asymptomatic hypertriglyceridemia associated with long-term low-dose rapamycin administration in a healthy middle-aged Labrador retriever.
evidence.quote: Within 15 days of discontinuing rapamycin treatment, and with no targeted lipemic intervention, the dog's lipemia and hypertriglyceridemia completely resolved.

question: In the longitudinal study in which 48 aged beagles (9-12 years) were assigned to control or antioxidant-fortified food crossed with a control or enriched environment, which group largely accounted for the treatment effects on size discrimination learning and reversal learning after 1 year?
answer: The combined treatment group (antioxidant-fortified food plus behavioral enrichment) largely accounted for the improvements.

evidence.title: Long-term treatment with antioxidants and a program of behavioral enrichment reduces age-dependent impairment in discrimination and reversal learning in beagle dogs.
evidence.quote: Both tasks were also improved by both the fortified food and the behavioral enrichment. However, in both instances the treatment effects largely reflected improved performance in the combined treatment group.

question: In the longitudinal study of lifetime 25% calorie restriction in 48 Labrador retrievers, did the authors conclude that there were differences between diet-restricted and control-fed dogs in the prevalence or severity of radiographic and histopathologic elbow osteoarthritis, and did the 1.8-year extension in median lifespan come with any additional incremental worsening of elbow disease?
answer: No. No differences in prevalence or severity of radiographic or histopathologic elbow OA were found between feeding groups, and the longer-lived restricted dogs showed no additional incremental worsening of elbow disease.

evidence.title: A longitudinal study of the influence of lifetime food restriction on development of osteoarthritis in the canine elbow.
evidence.quote: No differences in prevalence or severity of radiographic and histopathologic elbow OA were found between feeding groups. Diet restriction resulted in a 1.8-year extension in median lifespan but no additional incremental worsening of elbow disease.

review.issue: A flat 'No' is contradicted by the same abstract's Results ('Radiographic OA severity was greater for CF dogs at 6 years only, P<.05'); the quote is the authors' overall conclusion, so the question should ask what the study concluded and should also ask for the 'no additional incremental worsening' clause the answer already contains.

question: How many dogs in total (and per arm) will be enrolled and randomized in the TRIAD rapamycin trial, and what minimum difference in mean lifespan between treatment groups is the trial powered (at more than 80%) to detect?
answer: 580 dogs (290 rapamycin-treated, 290 placebo-treated); more than 80% power to detect a 6% or greater difference in mean lifespan.

evidence.title: Rapamycin as a potential intervention to promote longevity and extend healthspan in companion dogs
evidence.quote: A total of 580 dogs (n = 290 rapamycin-treated, n = 290 placebo-treated) will be enrolled and randomized, and for the primary outcome measure of survival time from randomization, the trial will have > 80% power to detect a 6% or greater difference in mean lifespan between treatment groups.

question: In the L-deprenyl beagle survival study, what proportions of dogs aged 10-15 years at the start of treatment survived to the end of the study in the L-deprenyl and placebo groups, and what did a later meta-analysis conclude when it reanalysed this dog study accounting for age at enrollment and sex?
answer: 12 of 15 (80%) L-deprenyl dogs versus 7 of 18 (39%) placebo dogs (P=0.017); after adjusting for age at enrollment and sex, the survival effect was no longer significant, though power was limited by small sample size.

evidence.title: Treatment with L-deprenyl prolongs life in elderly dogs.
evidence.quote: To assess whether L-deprenyl treatment begun in later life might enhance canine longevity in a fashion similar to that documented in rodents we also examined survival in a subset of elderly dogs who were between the ages of 10 and 15 yrs at the start of tablet administration and who received tablets for at least 6 months. In this subset, dogs in the L-deprenyl group survived longer (p < 0.05) than dogs in the placebo group. Twelve of 15 (80%) dogs in the L-deprenyl group survived to the conclusion of the study, in contrast to only 7 of 18 (39%) of the dogs who received placebo (P=0.017).

evidence.title: L-deprenyl extends lifespan across mammalian species: A meta-analysis of 22 longevity experiments.
evidence.quote: In addition to the meta-analysis, we reanalyzed a dog survival study by Ruehl et al. When accounting for age at enrollment and sex, the study no longer displayed a significant effect on survival, though power was limited by small sample size.

notes: Synthesis across the original 1997 survival study and its 2025 reanalysis.

question: In the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD) trial, what oral rapamycin dose and dosing frequency are used, for how long is treatment given, and how long is the post-treatment monitoring period?
answer: 0.15 mg/kg orally once weekly for 12 months, followed by a 24-month post-treatment monitoring period.

evidence.title: Rapamycin as a potential intervention to promote longevity and extend healthspan in companion dogs

evidence.quote: Compared to dogs within the lowest tertile of FI (less than 0.38), dogs within the highest tertile of FI (0.49 and above) had a 2-fold increase in risk of mortality (HR (95% CI) = 2.00 (1.17-3.40); p = 0.01) (Figure 3).

notes: Cross-paper synthesis: the CaniAge cut-off is justified by the tertile analysis in the EARS-FI development paper.

question: According to the design paper describing the Dog Aging Project as an open-data, community-science longitudinal study of ageing in companion dogs, which categories of data does the project plan to collect?
answer: Survey data, environmental information, electronic veterinary medical records, genome-wide sequence information, clinicopathology, and molecular phenotypes derived from blood cells, plasma and faecal samples.

evidence.title: An open science study of ageing in companion dogs.
evidence.quote: To take advantage of this opportunity, the Dog Aging Project will collect extensive survey data, environmental information, electronic veterinary medical records, genome-wide sequence information, clinicopathology and molecular phenotypes derived from blood cells, plasma and faecal samples.

question: In the Dog Aging Project precision cohort, one thousand dog-owner pairs were recruited into cohort strata. On which four variables were those strata based?
answer: Life stage, sex, size, and geography.

evidence.title: Rationale and design of the Dog Aging Project precision cohort: a multi-omic resource for longitudinal research in geroscience.
evidence.quote: One thousand dog-owner pairs were recruited into cohort strata based on life stage, sex, size, and geography.

question: In the cross-sectional analysis of 40,367 initial Dog Aging Project survey responses (2020-2022) on owner dietary choices, what percentage of owners fed a commercially prepared extruded dry diet (kibble) as their dog's primary diet component?

evidence.title: Dog and owner demographics impact dietary choices in Dog Aging Project cohort.
evidence.quote: Most owners (82%) fed a commercially prepared extruded dry diet (kibble) as the primary diet component.

question: The Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD) recruits dogs from Dog Aging Project participants. What is its trial design, and in which dogs does it test rapamycin?
answer: A parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial testing whether rapamycin prolongs lifespan and improves healthspan metrics in healthy, middle-aged dogs.

evidence.title: Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD): study design and rationale for a prospective, parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial of rapamycin in healthy middle-aged dogs from the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: The Test of Rapamycin In Aging Dogs (TRIAD) randomized clinical trial is a parallel-group, double-masked, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial that will test the ability of rapamycin to prolong lifespan and improve several healthspan metrics in healthy, middle-aged dogs recruited from Dog Aging Project participants.

question: In the Dog Aging Project analysis of owner-reported supplement use from enrollment surveys collected 2020-2022, what proportion of the 40,367 dogs received supplements, and which two supplement types were most common among supplemented dogs?
answer: 52% (20,993 of 40,367) received supplements; the most common were omega-3 fatty acids (57%) and joint supplements (56%).

evidence.title: Supplement use is common in Dog Aging Project participants, especially among dogs with orthopedic conditions, and varies by life stage.
evidence.quote: Half of the dogs in this study (20,993 of 40,367 [52%]) received supplements. Of those receiving supplements, the most common supplements administered were omega-3 fatty acids (11,934 [57%]) and joint supplements (11,810 [56%]).

question: In the Dog Aging Project comparison of owner-reported breed ancestry with genetic breed results for 5,673 dogs, what percentage of owners identified their dog's breed as matching the genetic report, and what was the most common explanation among owners who reported disagreement?
answer: 80% matched; among those disagreeing, most had dogs of a breed not included in the genetic reference panel.

evidence.title: Comparing owner reported and genetic breed identification reveals high concordance in a large cohort from the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: We find that 80% of dog owners identified their dog's breed as matching the genetic reports. Among those few who reported disagreement with the genetic results, the majority indicated having dogs belonging to a breed not included in the reference panel.

review.issue: Labelled numeric but the answer pairs a percentage with a categorical explanation (breed not in reference panel), so short_text describes it better.

question: In the Dog Aging Project study comparing owner-reported diagnoses from the Health and Life Experience Survey with veterinary electronic medical records across 20 disease categories, which category had the lowest agreement and which had the highest, with their agreement percentages?
answer: Lowest: dental/oral at 44%. Highest: endocrine, immune, and "other" categories at 99%.

evidence.title: Accuracy of owner-reported diagnoses for dogs enrolled in the Dog Aging Project as compared to veterinary electronic medical records.
evidence.quote: Agreement was highest in endocrine, immune, and "other" categories (99%) and lowest in dental/oral (44%).

question: In the retrospective analysis of Dog Aging Project End of Life Survey responses from 2020 through 2024, what proportion of owners reported pain and/or suffering as a reason for euthanasia, and what was the odds ratio associating recent veterinary consultation with reporting pain or suffering?
answer: 87% (7,764 of 8,955 owners); recent veterinary consultation OR 1.76 (95% CI 1.50-2.05).

evidence.title: Poor quality of life and recent veterinary consultation are associated with increased owner-perceived pain and/or suffering prior to euthanasia in dogs.
evidence.quote: Overall, 7,764 of 8,955 owners (87%) reported pain and/or suffering as a reason for euthanasia, with older owners, smaller dogs, and dogs < 5 years of age as factors that had lower frequency of pain as a reason for euthanasia.

evidence.title: Poor quality of life and recent veterinary consultation are associated with increased owner-perceived pain and/or suffering prior to euthanasia in dogs.
evidence.quote: Recent veterinary consultation was positively associated with pain or suffering (OR, 1.76; 95% CI, 1.50 to 2.05), and better quality of life was negatively associated with pain or suffering (OR, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.86 to 0.93).

question: In the validation of the Dog Aging Project End of Life Survey (EOLS), inter-rater reliability was assessed for three themes. Which theme had the highest reliability, and what were the kappa values for all three?
answer: Cause of death was highest (κ = 0.73); perimortem quality of life κ = 0.49; reason for euthanasia κ = 0.3.

evidence.title: Development and validation of a novel instrument to capture companion dog mortality data: the Dog Aging Project End of Life Survey.
evidence.quote: The EOLS had fair to substantial reliability for the 3 validation themes-cause of death (κ = 0.73; 95% CI, 0.5 to 0.95), perimortem quality of life (κ = 0.49; 95% CI, 0.26 to 0.73), and reason for euthanasia (κ = 0.3; 95% CI, 0.08 to 0.52)-and had no need for any substantial content alterations based on free-text analysis.

question: The Dog Aging Project precision cohort recruited one thousand dog-owner pairs for multi-omic profiling. From how many dogs did the project actually collect and process blood, urine, fecal, and hair samples in collaboration with primary care veterinarians?
answer: 976 dogs.

evidence.title: Rationale and design of the Dog Aging Project precision cohort: a multi-omic resource for longitudinal research in geroscience.
evidence.quote: In collaboration with primary care veterinarians, we collected and processed blood, urine, fecal, and hair samples from 976 dogs.

evidence.title: Protein Catabolites as Blood-Based Biomarkers of Aging Physiology: Findings From the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: Beginning in January of 2021, 976 dogs were recruited into the Precision Cohort, representing a wide diversity of dog age, genetics, and geography.

notes: Second evidence item corroborates the 976 figure from the first-year metabolome analysis of the same cohort.

question: In the Dog Aging Project analysis of owner-reported supplement use, how did the proportion of dogs receiving supplements change across owner-perceived overall health, from dogs rated in excellent health to those rated in very poor health?
answer: It rose from 45% among dogs in excellent health to 68% among dogs in very poor health.

evidence.title: Supplement use is common in Dog Aging Project participants, especially among dogs with orthopedic conditions, and varies by life stage.
evidence.quote: Dogs reported to be in poorer overall health were more likely to receive supplements compared to their counterparts reported to be in better health, with supplement use increasing from 45% among dogs in excellent health to 68% for those in very poor health.

question: In the Dog Aging Project study comparing owner-reported HLES diagnoses with veterinary electronic medical records, how was the sample of 350 dogs composed with respect to the five target disease categories, and why were 50 dogs added above the 300-dog target from the power analysis?
answer: 250 dogs with at least one target-disease-category diagnosis plus 100 dogs with none; the extra 50 allowed for an anticipated 16% dropout due to incomplete records.

evidence.title: Accuracy of owner-reported diagnoses for dogs enrolled in the Dog Aging Project as compared to veterinary electronic medical records.
evidence.quote: Our analysis suggested that a sample of 300 dogs would yield 90% power to detect whether HLES reports of dogs with no diseases in the TDCs matched VEMR records with no diseases in the TDCs better than expected by chance. Thus, to adequately assess agreement between VEMR data and the owner-reported HLES for the five TDCs, a total study sample of 350 dogs was randomly selected from among those eligible – 250 dogs with a minimum of one TDC diagnosis and 100 dogs without a TDC diagnosis – with the additional 50 above the 300-dog target included to account for an anticipated 16% dropout rate due to incomplete records.

question: In the second pilot validating the Dog Aging Project chronic diagnosis inventory (CDI) for documenting canine multimorbidity, which indexed condition was the only one whose inter-rater agreement was worse than chance, and what was its kappa?
answer: Periodontal disease (κ = −0.24).

evidence.title: Development and validation of a chronic diagnosis inventory that enables reliable documentation of canine multimorbidity in the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: Periodontal disease was the only condition with inter-rater agreement worse than chance agreement (κ = −0.24; P = .31).

question: According to the 2022 Annual Review 'Dog Models of Aging', what is the most notable limitation of laboratory models that studying aging in dogs could overcome?
answer: The ability to assess how aging-associated pathways influence aging in real-world environments similar to those experienced by humans.

evidence.title: Dog Models of Aging.
evidence.quote: We conclude that studying aging in dogs could overcome many limitations of laboratory models, most notably, the ability to assess how aging-associated pathways influence aging in real-world environments similar to those experienced by humans.

question: How does the 2023 GeroScience review on translational opportunities from veterinary biobanks define biobanking?
answer: The systematic collection, processing, storage, and distribution of biological material and associated data.

evidence.title: Banking on a new understanding: translational opportunities from veterinary biobanks.
evidence.quote: Biobanking, the systematic collection, processing, storage, and distribution of biological material and associated data has contributed to basic, clinical, and translational research by streamlining the management of high-quality biospecimens for biomarker discovery and validation.

question: In the 2009 perspective 'Comparative biology of aging' (Journals of Gerontology A), by roughly how much are dogs of different sizes said to differ in health span?
answer: By more than 50%.

evidence.title: Comparative biology of aging.
evidence.quote: Comparisons among dogs of different sizes, which differ by more than 50% in health span might also prove rewarding, as might novel species chosen because of their similarity to humans in certain key traits.

question: In the 2018 large-scale comparison of age-specific morbidity and mortality in humans and companion dogs (Aging Cell), which four chronic conditions common in human populations were found to be associated with similarly high levels of comorbidity in companion dogs?
answer: Obesity, arthritis, hypothyroidism, and diabetes.

evidence.title: The companion dog as a model for human aging and mortality.
evidence.quote: We find that many chronic conditions that commonly occur in human populations (obesity, arthritis, hypothyroidism, and diabetes), and which are associated with comorbidities, are also associated with similarly high levels of comorbidity in companion dogs.

question: According to the 2024 commentary on interdisciplinary collaboration between human and veterinary medicine (Veterinary Sciences), approximately what percentage of novel drugs fail to pass human clinical trials, and what fraction of those failures is attributed to unanticipated human toxicity?
answer: Approximately 89% fail; about half of those failures are due to unanticipated human toxicity.

evidence.title: Overcoming Challenges in Interdisciplinary Collaboration Between Human and Veterinary Medicine.
evidence.quote: Approximately 89% of novel drugs do not pass human clinical trials, with half of those failures due to unanticipated human toxicity [2].

question: In the 2018 comparison of human and canine patterns of age-specific morbidity and mortality, which three categories of cause of death were reported to show similar age trajectories in the two species?
answer: Neoplastic, congenital, and metabolic causes of death.

evidence.title: The companion dog as a model for human aging and mortality.
evidence.quote: We also find significant similarities in the effect of age on disease risk in humans and dogs, with neoplastic, congenital, and metabolic causes of death showing similar age trajectories between the two species.

question: In the 2024 GeroScience mini-review revisiting 'the hallmarks of aging' in domestic dogs, what two study-design recommendations does the author argue are important for dog aging studies?
answer: Include several breeds of dogs at differing ages, and apply age corrections for breeds with differing mean lifespans.

evidence.title: A revisiting of "the hallmarks of aging" in domestic dogs: current status of the literature.
evidence.quote: I also argue for the importance of dog aging studies to include several breeds of dogs at differing ages and for age corrections for breeds with differing mean lifespans throughout.

question: In the translational geroscience research pipeline described in the 2018 review 'Translational Geroscience: From invertebrate models to companion animal and human interventions', after an intervention is discovered in invertebrate model systems, which three kinds of models are used to characterize it before validation in vertebrates?
answer: Other invertebrate model systems (evolutionary translation), models of genetic diversity, and disease models.

evidence.title: Translational Geroscience: From invertebrate models to companion animal and human interventions.
evidence.quote: Beginning in invertebrate model systems, interventions are discovered and then characterized using other invertebrate model systems (evolutionary translation), models of genetic diversity, and disease models.

question: The 2017 review 'The companion dog as a unique translational model for aging' states that dogs and humans co-evolved and share recent evolutionary selection processes. What example of such a shared selection process does it give?
answer: Adaptation to digest starch-rich diets.

evidence.title: The companion dog as a unique translational model for aging.
evidence.quote: Dogs and humans co-evolved and share recent evolutionary selection processes, such as adaptation to digest starch-rich diets.

question: The 2026 mBio review of the canine gut microbiome as a translational model for human health and aging lists several major limitations of the canine system. What are they?
answer: The need for breed and body-size stratification; heterogeneous diet and husbandry; incomplete treatment histories; lack of routinely available gnotobiotic canine systems; and gaps in canine-specific reference resources.

evidence.title: The canine gut microbiome as a translational model for human health and aging.
evidence.quote: Major limitations include the need for breed and body-size stratification, heterogeneous diet and husbandry, incomplete treatment histories, the lack of routinely available gnotobiotic canine systems, and gaps in canine-specific reference resources.

question: In its introduction, the 2024 commentary on overcoming challenges in collaboration between human and veterinary medicine lists four reasons why companion animals may be valuable for bridging preclinical and human clinical trials. What are they?
answer: They naturally develop diseases resembling human conditions; they share their owners' environment and lifestyle, reflecting human environmental variability; their use in drug trials is less ethically controversial than laboratory animals; their life expectancy has increased with veterinary care and nutrition.

evidence.title: Overcoming Challenges in Interdisciplinary Collaboration Between Human and Veterinary Medicine.
evidence.quote: Firstly, these animals naturally develop diseases that closely resemble human conditions, making them highly relevant models for studying these diseases and testing potential treatments [5]. Secondly, assuming companion animals are kept at a close distance to their owner for mainly entertainment, interest, affection, or for show or sporting events [6], companion animals experience the unique environment and lifestyle of their owners, which reflects the environmental variability in humans.

evidence.title: Overcoming Challenges in Interdisciplinary Collaboration Between Human and Veterinary Medicine.
evidence.quote: Thirdly, companion animals are not subject to the same degree of as laboratory animals, making their involvement in drug trials a potentially less ethically controversial alternative. Finally, similar to humans, the life expectancy of companion animals has increased due to advancements in veterinary medicine, preventative care, and better nutrition.

notes: The two quotes are consecutive sentences in the introduction; split into two evidence items only to respect the 700-character quote limit. The source text contains the typo 'the same degree of as laboratory animals' verbatim.

question: In the Dog Aging Project Precision Cohort analysis reporting that dogs and humans share plasma metabolite biomarkers of all-cause mortality, what was the average follow-up time for the 937 dogs, and what was the range of average follow-up times among participants in the human studies used for comparison?
answer: Dogs were followed for an average of 2.6 years (maximum 3.9 years); average follow-up in the human studies ranged from 8.0 to 22.5 years.

evidence.title: Dogs and humans share biomarkers of mortality.
evidence.quote: The mortality analysis in the Precision Cohort involved 104 deaths among 937 dogs that were followed for an average of 2.6 years (maximum = 3.9 years). By contrast, average follow-up times among participants reported in the human studies ranged from 8.0 to 22.5 years and included cohorts that have been followed for as long as 28 years (Supplementary Information).

question: The 2024 commentary on collaboration between human and veterinary medicine notes that dogs are 'small animals' in veterinary practice yet are called 'large animals' in translational research. According to the commentary, what does 'large animal' mean in the translational research context, and why are dogs labelled that way?
answer: In translational research, 'large animals' are species larger than common laboratory rodents (mice and rats); dogs are labelled large animals because they offer a more relevant physiological model for human responses, not because of their size relative to livestock.

evidence.title: Overcoming Challenges in Interdisciplinary Collaboration Between Human and Veterinary Medicine.
evidence.quote: However, this classification system does not apply to translational research and animal models, as large animals are referred to as species larger than common laboratory rodents, such as mice and rats. For example, dogs are referenced as "large animals" in this context, not because of their size relative to livestock, but because they offer a more relevant physiological model and better stimulation for human responses [57,58,59,60].

question: In the Dog Aging Project Precision Cohort survey of the plasma metabolome (first year of sampling), approximately what percentage of measured metabolites showed an effect of age?
answer: Approximately 36% of measured metabolites.

evidence.title: Protein Catabolites as Blood-Based Biomarkers of Aging Physiology: Findings From the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: We identified effects of age on approximately 36% of measured metabolites.

question: In the Dog Aging Project cross-sectional inflammaging pilot study of 47 healthy companion dogs of various breeds, which serum cytokines were positively associated with age, and which hematological parameter was negatively associated with age?
answer: IL-6, IL-8 and TNF-α were positively associated with age; lymphocyte count was negatively associated with age.

evidence.title: The companion dog as a model for inflammaging: a cross-sectional pilot study.
evidence.quote: Serum IL-6, IL-8, and TNF-α concentrations were all positively associated with age. Lymphocyte count was negatively associated with age.

question: In the multi-omic study profiling whole-blood gene expression and plasma protein abundance in 40 laboratory beagles across young, old and geriatric life stages, how many genes and how many proteins significantly changed in abundance with aging, and on which pathways did they converge?
answer: 816 genes and 40 proteins; converging on DNA repair, collagen processing, and inflammation pathways.

evidence.title: Multi-omic analysis of canine aging uncovers conserved aging pathways.
evidence.quote: We identified 816 genes and 40 proteins that significantly changed in abundance during aging, converging on pathways involved in DNA repair, collagen processing, and inflammation.

question: In the year-long study comparing a fresh, human-grade food with an extruded kibble diet in 22 geriatric Alaskan sled dogs, which serum metabolite groups were decreased in the fresh-food (treatment) group?
answer: Advanced glycation end products, fatty acid synthesis, and creatinine.

evidence.title: Serum Metabolomics of Senior Dogs Fed a Fresh, Human-Grade Food or an Extruded Kibble Diet.
evidence.quote: The treatment group had decreased advanced glycation end products, fatty acid synthesis, and creatinine.

question: In the 24-week restricted-feeding study of a high-protein, high-fiber diet in 12 overweight spayed female dogs, what percentage of initial body weight was lost, and which two inflammatory markers decreased with weight loss?
answer: 31.2% of initial body weight; C-reactive protein and interleukin-6 decreased (along with triglycerides, leptin and insulin).

evidence.title: Weight loss and high-protein, high-fiber diet consumption impact blood metabolite profiles, body composition, voluntary physical activity, fecal microbiota, and fecal metabolites of adult dogs.
evidence.quote: After 24 wk, dogs lost 31.2% of initial BW and had 1.43 ± 0.73% weight loss per week. BCS decreased (P < 0.0001) by 2.7 units, fat mass decreased (P < 0.0001) by 3.1 kg, and fat percentage decreased (P < 0.0001) by 11.7% with weight loss. Many serum metabolites and hormones were altered, with triglycerides, leptin, insulin, C-reactive protein, and interleukin-6 decreasing (P < 0.05) with weight loss.

question: In the Dog Aging Project Precision Cohort plasma metabolome study that identified post-translationally modified amino acids (ptmAAs) as a novel biomarker of age, what clinical physiological measure mediated about half of the age effect on ptmAA levels, and was the ptmAA-age association robust to diet?
answer: Clinical measures of kidney function mediated about half of the age effect; yes, the ptmAA covariation with age was robust to diet.

evidence.title: Protein Catabolites as Blood-Based Biomarkers of Aging Physiology: Findings From the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: The ptmAAs, which are generated by protein hydrolysis, covaried both with age and with other biomarkers of amino acid metabolism, and in a way that was robust to diet. Clinical measures of kidney function mediated about half of the age effect on ptmAA levels.

question: In the Dog Aging Project Precision cohort gut microbiome study (over 900 dogs, fecal shotgun metagenomics), what kind of model did the age-associated gradual shifts in microbiome composition support developing, and which human cohort was used to test whether human age-associated microbial patterns are recapitulated in dogs?
answer: A metagenomics-based population-level model for canine age prediction from microbial signatures; the Lifelines-DEEP human cohort.

evidence.title: Mapping the canine gut microbiome: insights from the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: In addition, we find age-associated gradual shifts in microbiome composition, supporting the development of a metagenomics-based population-level model for canine age prediction based on microbial signatures. We further examined which age-associated microbial patterns observed in humans are recapitulated in dogs by comparing our cohort with the Lifelines-DEEP cohort.

question: In the large-scale global metabolomic profiling of companion dogs of varying sizes and ages from three US cities, which factor gave the strongest signal in the metabolome, and after controlling for it, which metabolic pathway was associated with body weight and in which size class were its metabolites higher?
answer: Geographic location (stronger than age, breed or sex); tryptophan metabolism, with small dogs having significantly higher levels of tryptophan pathway metabolites.

evidence.title: Tryptophan metabolism is differently regulated between large and small dogs.
evidence.quote: We found a surprisingly strong location signal in the metabolome, stronger in fact than any signal related to age, breed, or sex. However, after controlling for the effects of location, tryptophan metabolism emerged as significantly associated with weight of the dogs, with small dogs having significantly higher levels of tryptophan pathway metabolites.

evidence.title: THE EFFECTS OF AGE AND SIZE ON THE COMPANION DOG METABOLOME: ROLES OF TRYPTOPHAN AND FATTY ACID METABOLISM
evidence.quote: After controlling for this location effect, we found a strong signal of amino acid metabolism, specifically tryptophan metabolism, associated with weight in the dog where metabolites in the tryptophan metabolism pathway were always higher in small, long-lived dogs.

question: In the preprint characterizing age-associated hematologic and serum cytokine profiles in intact laboratory Beagles, how many dogs were studied over what age span, and which sex showed extensive age-dependent inflammatory restructuring of cytokines?
answer: 80 intact laboratory Beagles spanning 1 to 11 years; intact males showed extensive age-dependent inflammatory restructuring, whereas females showed restricted fluctuations.

evidence.title: Sex-dimorphic immune trajectories across the canine lifespan and early-life signatures of geroprotective interventions
evidence.quote: Here, we characterize the age-associated hematologic and serum cytokine profiles of 80 intact laboratory Beagles spanning 1 to 11 years. Contrary to classical linear models of immunosenescence and inflammaging, we reveal that canine immune aging is highly dynamic and sexually dimorphic. While absolute leukocyte counts declined continuously, cytokine remodeling was sex-specific: intact males exhibited extensive age-dependent inflammatory restructuring, whereas females demonstrated restricted fluctuations.

question: In the Dog Aging Project Precision Cohort targeted plasma metabolome study (the ptmAA biomarker paper), how many of the six measured carnitines associated strongly with age, and which was the only one negatively associated with age?
answer: 4 of the 6 carnitines; γ-butyrobetaine was the only one negatively associated with age (the other 3 were positively associated).

evidence.title: Protein Catabolites as Blood-Based Biomarkers of Aging Physiology: Findings From the Dog Aging Project.
evidence.quote: However, of the six carnitines measured, four associated strongly with age, with all but one, γ‐butyrobetaine, positively associated with age.

notes: Full-text discussion detail; the aqueous panel excluded hydrophilic lipids.

question: In the immunophenotyping study of peripheral blood lymphocytes in 160 healthy dogs aged 1 to 17 years and 365 dogs with tumors, how did the CD4:CD8 ratio change with age in healthy dogs, and how did the ratio in tumor-bearing dogs compare with age-matched controls?
answer: It decreased significantly with age in healthy dogs, whereas dogs with tumors had a significantly higher CD4:CD8 ratio than age-matched controls.

evidence.title: Alterations of lymphocyte subpopulations in healthy dogs with aging and in dogs with cancer.
evidence.quote: The CD4:CD8 ratio showed a significant age-related decrease. In contrast, dogs with tumors possessed significantly lower absolute numbers and relative percentages of all lymphocyte phenotypes, while the CD4:CD8 ratio was significantly higher than in age-matched controls.

notes: Counter-intuitive detail: tumor-bearing dogs show a higher, not lower, CD4:CD8 ratio than age-matched controls.

question: In the year-long serum metabolomics study of geriatric Alaskan sled dogs switched from extruded kibble to a fresh, human-grade food, when did the largest change in the serum metabolome occur relative to the rest of the year?
answer: Within the first month of consuming the treatment diet; changes over the rest of the year were modest by comparison.

evidence.title: Serum Metabolomics of Senior Dogs Fed a Fresh, Human-Grade Food or an Extruded Kibble Diet.
evidence.quote: There was a large change in the serum metabolome within the first month of consuming the treatment diet, with changes in the metabolome over the rest of the year being modest in comparison to the first month.

question: In the 2016 study of multimorbidity in over 2,000 companion dogs attending private veterinary clinics in England, how did the number of diagnoses relate to age, and did body weight or breed have a significant effect on morbidity number?
answer: The number of diagnoses increased significantly with age; there was no significant effect of body weight or breed on morbidity number.

evidence.title: Multiple morbidities in companion dogs: a novel model for investigating age-related disease.
evidence.quote: In common with humans, we find that the number of diagnoses increases significantly with age in dogs. However, we find no significant weight or breed effects on morbidity number.

question: In the Dog Aging Project analysis of multimorbidity as a predictor of mortality, based on owner-reported data from over 50,000 dogs, which three conditions were highly prevalent across the multimorbidity combinations identified?
answer: Osteoarthritis, overweight, and cancer.

evidence.title: Multimorbidity as a predictor of mortality in companion dogs.
evidence.quote: Through classifying multimorbidities, we found that almost all either exhibit a synergistic effect or are driven by a single, predominant condition. In both cases, osteoarthritis, overweight, and cancer were highly prevalent throughout.

question: In the study comparing causes of death among over 40,000 sterilized and reproductively intact companion dogs, what association did sterilization have with lifespan, and which cause of death did it decrease and which did it increase?
answer: Sterilization was strongly associated with increased lifespan; it decreased the risk of death from infectious disease but increased the risk of death from cancer.

evidence.title: Reproductive capability is associated with lifespan and cause of death in companion dogs.
evidence.quote: We found that sterilization was strongly associated with an increase in lifespan, and while it decreased risk of death from some causes, such as infectious disease, it actually increased risk of death from others, such as cancer.

question: In the study of lifetime medical histories of 345 Rottweilers, what percentage of extreme-aged dogs (alive at the 95th percentile age at death, 13.3 years or older) died of cancer, compared with dogs of usual longevity (9-10 years)?
answer: 19% of extreme-aged dogs died of cancer versus 82% of dogs with usual longevity.

evidence.title: Exceptional longevity in pet dogs is accompanied by cancer resistance and delayed onset of major diseases.
evidence.quote: Extreme aged dogs (alive at the 95th percentile age at death for the study population, > or =13.3 years) were compared with a usual longevity group (9-10 years). Exceptional longevity in Rottweiler dogs was accompanied by a significant delay in the onset of major life-threatening diseases; 76% of extreme aged dogs remained free of all major diseases during the first 9 years of life. Only 19% of extreme aged dogs died of cancer versus 82% of dogs with usual longevity (p <.0001).

question: Among the 652 golden retrievers with known age that underwent necropsy at a veterinary academic center between 1989 and 2016, what proportion were determined to have died because of cancer, and how did the median age at death of dogs dying of cancer compare with those dying of other causes?
answer: 65.0% (424 of 652) died of cancer; median age at death was 9.83 years for cancer deaths versus 6.93 years for deaths from other causes.

evidence.title: Association of cancer-related mortality, age and gonadectomy in golden retriever dogs at a veterinary academic center (1989-2016).
evidence.quote: 424 of the 652 (65.0%) were determined to have died because of cancer. The median age for dying of a cause other than cancer was 6.93 years while those dying of cancer had a median age of 9.83 years (p<0.0001).

question: Before a veterinary clinical trial, 40 companion dogs with no history of cardiac pathology (at least 6 years old and at least 18 kg) were screened by Doppler echocardiography. How many were diagnosed with valvular regurgitation, how many of those were severe enough to be excluded from the trial, and in how many was a heart murmur detected by auscultation?
answer: 11 dogs had valvular regurgitation; 7 were severe enough to warrant exclusion; a heart murmur was detected by auscultation in only 1 case.

evidence.title: Asymptomatic heart valve dysfunction in healthy middle-aged companion dogs and its implications for cardiac aging.
evidence.quote: Eleven dogs from this cohort were diagnosed with valvular regurgitation by echocardiography, and seven of these cases were of sufficient severity to warrant exclusion from the clinical trial. In only one case was a heart murmur detected by auscultation.

question: In the 2018 analysis of sex differences in aging that used two large independent databases of companion dog longevity and causes of death, how did the survival advantage by sex differ between intact and neutered dogs?
answer: Among intact dogs there was a small male survival advantage, whereas among neutered dogs there was a clear female survival advantage.

evidence.title: Do Female Dogs Age Differently Than Male Dogs?
evidence.quote: When broken down by neutering status, we discovered a small male advantage in survival among intact dogs but a clear female survival advantage among neutered dogs.

question: In the Italian multi-centre study of 4957 dogs that died between 2004 and 2020 (records from 9 veterinary teaching hospitals and 2 public health institutions), what was the most frequent cause of death when classified by pathophysiologic process, and what was the most frequent when classified by organ system?
answer: By pathophysiologic process, neoplasia (34.0%), more frequent in large breeds; by organ system, diseases of the renal/urinary system (15.0%).

evidence.title: Factors related to longevity and mortality of dogs in Italy.
evidence.quote: The most frequent COD by PP was neoplasia (34.0%), which occurred more frequently in large breeds, namely German shepherd, Labrador retriever and Boxer. Degenerative diseases mostly affected small-sized dogs like Miniature pinscher and Dachshund. Regarding the OS involved, diseases of the renal/urinary system were most frequently responsible for COD (15.0%), prevalently degenerative and inflammatory/infectious.

question: In the analysis of owner-reported lifespan and cause of death across 118 breeds (more than 40,000 dogs, restricted to completed birth cohorts to remove right-censoring bias), how did the percentage of old-age mortality and the proportional cancer mortality change with increasing breed body size?
answer: The percentage of old-age mortality decreased with increasing body size, while large size significantly increased proportional cancer mortality.

evidence.title: How size and genetic diversity shape lifespan across breeds of purebred dogs.
evidence.quote: Old age lifespan, as well as the percentage of old age mortality, decreased with increasing body size and increased with increasing genetic diversity. The lifespan of dogs dying of cancer followed the same patterns, but while large size significantly increased proportional cancer mortality, we could not detect a significant signal for lowered cancer mortality with increasing diversity.

question: In the survival analysis of 20,970 privately owned dogs from three independent primary care veterinary clinics in the United States, was gonadectomy associated with longer lifespan, in which sex was the effect stronger, and was the advantage retained in females that had already survived to ages 5 and 8 years?
answer: Yes, gonadectomy was associated with longer lifespan, more strongly in females than males, and the advantage was conserved in gonadectomized females that lived to at least 5 and 8 years.

evidence.title: Lifespan of companion dogs seen in three independent primary care veterinary clinics in the United States.
evidence.quote: Gonadectomy was associated with a longer lifespan, with the effect being stronger in females than in males. This lifespan advantage was conserved in gonadectomized female dogs that lived to at least ages 5 and 8 years.

question: The 2016 English clinic study of multimorbidity in over 2,000 companion dogs found that breeds differ in longevity yet show similar age-related trajectories of morbidity number. What did the authors suggest is the likely source of the variation in lifespan across breeds?
answer: Differences in the age of onset of disease, rather than differences in the age-related trajectory of morbidity accumulation.

evidence.title: Multiple morbidities in companion dogs: a novel model for investigating age-related disease.
evidence.quote: This surprising result reveals that while breeds may vary in their average longevity and causes of death, their age-related trajectories of morbidities differ little, suggesting that age of onset of disease may be the source of variation in lifespan across breeds.

question: In the VetCompass Australia study of Bullmastiff demography, longevity and mortality, what odds ratio was reported for the effect of neutering on death from urogenital disorders, and which specific diagnosis accounted for 41.7% of urogenital-related deaths?
answer: Neutering decreased the risk of urogenital death with an odds ratio of 0.14; pyometra accounted for 41.7% of urogenital-related deaths.

evidence.title: The Demography, Longevity and Mortality of Bullmastiffs Attending Veterinary Practices in Australia.
evidence.quote: The current study revealed that neutering decreased the risk (OR: 0.14) of death by a urogenital disorder, specifically pyometra which accounted for 41.7% of urogenital-related deaths.

question: In the echocardiographic screening study of 40 healthy middle-aged companion dogs (at least 6 years old, at least 18 kg) that revealed asymptomatic valvular regurgitation, which serum biochemistry analyte was significantly higher in dogs with moderate to severe valvular regurgitation than in the rest of the cohort?
answer: Serum alkaline phosphatase.

evidence.title: Asymptomatic heart valve dysfunction in healthy middle-aged companion dogs and its implications for cardiac aging.
evidence.quote: Serum alkaline phosphatase levels were significantly higher in the dogs with moderate to severe valvular regurgitation compared to the rest of the cohort.

question: Two owner-based mortality surveys of purebred dogs in the UK reported leading causes of death: the questionnaire survey sent in 2004 to members of breed clubs of Kennel Club-recognised breeds (15,881 deaths) and the survey of dogs registered with the Kennel Club in 2014 (5663 deceased dogs). What was the single most commonly reported cause of death in each survey, with its percentage?
answer: 2004 breed-club survey: cancer (27%), followed by old age (18%). 2014 Kennel Club survey: old age (13.8%), followed by unspecified cancer (8.7%).

evidence.title: Methods and mortality results of a health survey of purebred dogs in the UK.
evidence.quote: The most common causes of death were cancer (n=4282, 27%), "old age" (n=2830, 18%) and cardiac conditions (n=1770, 11%).

evidence.title: Longevity and mortality in Kennel Club registered dog breeds in the UK in 2014.
evidence.quote: The most commonly reported causes of death were old age (13.8%), unspecified cancer (8.7%) and heart failure (4.9%); with 5.1% of deaths reported as unknown cause.

notes: Synthesis across two surveys; the leading reported cause differs (cancer vs old age), partly reflecting how cancer was coded (unspecified vs any cancer).

review.issue: Question stem calls both surveys 'surveys of UK Kennel Club registered dogs', but the 2004 survey covered dogs owned by breed-club members of KC-recognised breeds, not (necessarily) KC-registered dogs; only the 2014 survey was of KC-registered dogs.
